titleEn: The pub as Britain's third place, and why so many are closing
facts: The pub, short for public house, is a licensed drinking establishment that first took its modern name in late 17th-century England.

The Campaign for Real Ale defines a pub by four features: open to the public without membership, serves draught beer or cider without requiring food, has an indoor area not laid out for meals, and allows drinks to be bought at the bar.
Pubs have long functioned as community rooms for quiz nights, darts and pool teams, wakes, union meetings and football supporters' clubs.
The number of pubs has fallen sharply since the 2000s as drinking habits, prices and supermarket alcohol changed, with rural pubs especially vulnerable.
Working men's clubs, a related institution, were created in the 19th century as member-run social clubs with cheap beer and entertainment.
exampleEn: A village pub hosts the darts team on Tuesdays, the quiz on Thursdays and a wake on Saturday, and the landlord knows which regulars take milk.
qualificationEn: The 'local' is a nostalgic idea as much as a description: many pubs now depend on food and tourism, some are run by their communities, and British drinking patterns have changed a lot since the smoking ban of 2007.

titleEn: Bonfire Night: fireworks, effigies and an old plot
facts: Guy Fawkes Night, on 5 November, commemorates the failure of the 1605 Gunpowder Plot, when Catholic conspirators planned to blow up the Houses of Parliament and King James I.
An Act of Parliament in 1605 made the date an annual thanksgiving, and bonfires were lit to celebrate the king's survival.
Bonfires are still lit on 5 November with fireworks and, in many places, an effigy called a 'guy'; children once collected 'a penny for the guy'.
Some towns keep rowdier local traditions, such as the Lewes bonfires with their costumes and fireworks, or the tar-barrel rolling at Ottery St Mary.
Over time the anti-Catholic edge has faded for most participants, and the night is now a family and neighbourhood event, though sectarian tensions survive in a few places.
exampleEn: A suburban street gathers in a back garden on 5 November for sparklers, soup and a small fireworks display while the children compare their guys.
qualificationEn: Bonfire Night is a mainly British tradition with strong regional variety; in Scotland, Northern Ireland and parts of England the date overlaps with other commemorations, and safety rules have made private fireworks less common.

titleEn: Welsh is back in the classroom, on the signs and in the census
facts: Welsh is a Celtic language and, according to the 2021 census, 538,300 people in Wales aged three and over (17.8%) could speak it.
The Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011 gave Welsh official status in Wales, and Welsh and English are both official languages of the Senedd.
Welsh-medium education is the main engine of revival: many children from English-speaking homes now attend Welsh-medium schools and become fluent there.
Bilingual road signs, documents and the broadcaster S4C make the language visible in daily life, not only in classrooms.
The Welsh Government has a target of one million Welsh speakers by 2050, and language planning now covers workplaces, health services and newcomers.
exampleEn: A child in Cardiff answers the register in Welsh, watches S4C cartoons at home and sees 'Araf' painted on the road outside school.
qualificationEn: Welsh is far from secure: it is a minority language in parts of its own heartland, the proportion of speakers varies enormously by county, and growth in Welsh-medium schools has not always produced confident adult speakers.

titleEn: The Twelfth: parades, bonfires and memory in Northern Ireland
facts: The Twelfth, on 12 July, is an Ulster Protestant celebration of the Battle of the Boyne in 1690, when William of Orange defeated the Catholic James II.
The Orange Order, founded in 1795, organises parades of lodges and accompanying marching bands, and streets are decorated with Union flags and bunting.
On the Eleventh Night, large bonfires are lit in loyalist areas, some several storeys high.
The day is a public holiday in Northern Ireland and a major expression of unionist identity, but many parade routes pass through or near Catholic neighbourhoods and have been contested.
Parades are regulated by the Parades Commission, and disputes over routes can dominate local politics for months.
exampleEn: A band from a small town practises for months, then marches on the Twelfth behind a lodge banner while spectators line the main street.
qualificationEn: The Twelfth means very different things to unionists and nationalists: many Protestants see it as heritage and family tradition rather than a sectarian statement, while many Catholics experience it as intimidation, and describing it accurately requires holding both.

titleEn: 'Craic' is not an old Irish word, and that is the point
facts: 'Craic' (also spelled 'crack') means news, gossip, fun, entertainment and enjoyable conversation, especially in Ireland.
The word is not an ancient Gaelic inheritance: the Scots and English 'crack' was borrowed into Irish in the mid-20th century, and the Irish spelling was then reborrowed into English.
'What's the craic?' means 'How are you?' or 'What's happening?', and 'the craic was ninety' means the evening was excellent.
The word became a marketing slogan for Irish pubs and tourism in the 1990s, and 'ceol agus craic' (music and fun) is a standard pub phrase.
It suggests a social ideal in which conversation, humour and company matter more than planning or spending.
exampleEn: A visitor asks 'What's the craic?' on entering a pub, and the answer is a ten-minute account of a cousin's wedding rather than a simple 'fine'.
qualificationEn: 'Craic' is used everywhere in Ireland in English, but the Gaelic spelling is modern; Irish speakers do not necessarily use it, and the idea that craic is uniquely Irish is a marketing construction as much as a description.

titleEn: The Irish session: tunes in the corner, no stage
facts: A session is an informal gathering of musicians playing Irish traditional music, usually in a pub corner rather than on a stage.
The core repertoire is dance tunes, reels, jigs, hornpipes and polkas, played in sets of several tunes without a fixed arrangement.
Typical instruments are fiddle, flute, tin whistle, uilleann pipes, accordion, concertina, banjo and bodhrán; players join in when they know the tune.
Sessions have etiquette: a player starts a set, others follow, and approval is often a quiet nod rather than applause.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, founded in 1951, runs classes and the Fleadh Cheoil competitions that feed the session tradition.
exampleEn: On a Tuesday night six musicians sit around a table in a West Clare pub; a fiddler starts a reel and the others join at the second phrase without anyone counting in.
qualificationEn: Sessions range from tourist-friendly pub nights to serious players-only gatherings, and the 'authentic' session is partly a revival construction; many young musicians learn from recordings as well as from older players.

titleEn: The Gaeltacht: paying people to keep Irish alive
facts: The Gaeltacht is the set of districts where the Irish government recognises Irish as the predominant home language, first officially defined in the 1920s.
Irish is the first official language of Ireland, and about 1.9 million people can speak it, but only a small minority use it daily outside school.
A 2015 study found that Irish was spoken daily by at least two-thirds of the population in only a small number of Gaeltacht districts, and the language is declining in many of them.
State policy supports the Gaeltacht through grants, Irish-language schools, Údarás na Gaeltachta and a dedicated radio station, but jobs and housing remain scarce.
Gaeltacht summer colleges bring thousands of teenagers to live with Irish-speaking families, a formative experience for many Irish adults.
exampleEn: A Dublin teenager spends three weeks in a Connemara homestay, is asked to speak only Irish at breakfast, and comes home with a cúpla focal and a new accent.
qualificationEn: The Gaeltacht is not a single place or experience: some districts have strong daily Irish, others are effectively English-speaking, and the boundary is administrative as much as linguistic.

titleEn: The GAA: parish teams, amateur rules and a national code
facts: The Gaelic Athletic Association was founded in 1884 to promote Irish sports, above all hurling and Gaelic football, and now has over 500,000 members.
Clubs are organised by parish and county, so local identity is built into the competition: players represent where they come from, not a market.
The games are amateur: players are not paid, and rules on payments and transfers have caused repeated conflict.
Hurling is played with an ash stick (hurl) and a small ball (sliotar), with one point over the crossbar and three for a goal, and is often described as one of the fastest field games in the world.
The GAA also promotes Irish music, dance and the Irish language, and its grounds, especially Croke Park, are national symbols.
exampleEn: A village of 500 people fields a hurling team, and the whole parish turns out for the county final; the players train after work and are back at work on Monday.
qualificationEn: The GAA is amateur but highly organised and commercial at the top, and its history includes nationalist politics and exclusion; not all Irish people follow Gaelic games, especially in Dublin and among newer communities.

titleEn: La bise: how many kisses depends on where you are
facts: La bise is the French greeting of touching cheeks and making a light kiss sound, usually without lip contact.
The number of kisses varies by region: two is common in much of the north, while three or four are usual in parts of the south and west.
The greeting is governed by unwritten rules: it is common between friends, family and colleagues in informal settings, while a handshake is safer in business and with strangers.
It can take time: in a room of ten acquaintances, everyone may be expected to greet everyone else individually.
The COVID-19 pandemic interrupted the habit, and some workplaces and schools have kept a handshake or a verbal greeting since.
exampleEn: A Parisian meeting a friend's parents offers two kisses; a visitor from Marseille offers three, and the resulting pause is a small social negotiation.
qualificationEn: La bise is highly variable and not universal: older, rural and southern habits differ from Parisian ones, men sometimes shake hands instead, and many people dislike it, so there is no single French rule.

titleEn: Terroir: why French food is argued by place
facts: Terroir means the combination of soil, climate, tradition and human skill that gives a product its character, a French idea that has become a global marketing tool.
The appellation d'origine contrôlée (AOC) system, formalised in 1935, certifies that a product's production and processing take place in a defined area using recognised methods.
AOC covers wine, cheese, butter, meat and other products, and the rules can specify grape varieties, yields, ageing and even harvest size.
The system began as a response to fraud and overproduction in the wine trade, and it turned place names into legal guarantees.
Terroir is also a social idea: it ties producers to landscapes and local identities and is used to defend small producers against industrial food.
exampleEn: A cheesemaker in the Comté region cannot simply claim the name: the milk must come from a defined area, the cows must be fed in specific ways, and inspectors check the cellars.
qualificationEn: Terroir is partly a romantic story: industrial agriculture also has regional styles, the AOC system has been criticised for protecting incumbents, and many French products sold as traditional are recent inventions.

titleEn: The French café is a room for watching the street
facts: The café is a central French social institution: coffee is drunk quickly at the counter, while a table on the terrace is rented by the hour for conversation and people-watching.
Prices often differ between the counter, the table inside and the terrace, and the bill is a contract about how long you are welcome to stay.
Cafés served as meeting places for writers, politicians and workers, and the existentialists of Saint-Germain-des-Prés made the Left Bank café a global image.
The smoking ban of 2008 changed the atmosphere and the economics of the terrace, and many cafés now serve more food than coffee.
The bistro, a smaller eating place with a short menu, developed alongside the café and shares its social role.
exampleEn: A retired man orders a small espresso at the bar, reads the newspaper, greets the owner and is gone in ten minutes, while a student nurses a café crème on the terrace for two hours.
qualificationEn: Café culture is strongest in cities and tourist areas; rural France has lost many cafés, and the 'terrace as theatre' image is partly a Parisian export that other regions do not recognise.

titleEn: Grandes écoles and the making of French elites
facts: Grandes écoles are elite French higher-education institutions that run alongside the public university system.
Entry is usually by competitive examination after two years of preparatory classes rather than by open admission.
The most famous include the École Polytechnique, founded in 1794, and the École nationale d'administration (ENA), created in 1945 to train senior civil servants.
Their graduates dominate the senior civil service, business and politics and are known as énarques, polytechniciens and normaliens.

Critics say the system reproduces inequality: preparatory classes and the grandes écoles draw disproportionately from privileged families, and ENA was replaced in 2022 by a new institute after criticism of elitism.
exampleEn: A lycée student from a provincial town enters a Paris lycée for two years of prépa, then sits a week of written and oral exams hoping for a place at a grande école.
qualificationEn: The grandes écoles are not one system: engineering, business and humanities schools differ greatly, some are public and some private, and most French students never encounter them at all.

titleEn: Going Dutch: splitting the bill as a social philosophy
facts: 'Going Dutch' means each person pays their own share, and in the Netherlands this is a normal, unembarrassed part of social life.
The phrase is older and more complicated than the practice suggests: it was originally an English slur implying Dutch stinginess, and it entered English in the 19th century.
Dutch friends commonly split restaurant bills precisely, use payment request apps such as Tikkie, and keep track of small debts without treating them as insults.
The habit fits a wider culture of directness and equality: asking who owes what is considered practical rather than rude.
Birthdays show the same pattern: guests are often expected to bring a small gift and to congratulate the birthday person's family members in a set order.
exampleEn: After dinner with friends, one person pays the bill and sends a Tikkie request for everyone's exact share; nobody suggests that the payer should cover it.
qualificationEn: The stingy Dutchman is an unfair, outdated stereotype; many Dutch people happily treat friends, and the split-bill habit varies by generation, region and setting.

titleEn: Gezelligheid: the Dutch word for a room that works
facts: Gezelligheid is a Dutch concept for a warm, convivial atmosphere shared with others; the adjective gezellig describes a person, room or evening that produces it.
It is notoriously hard to translate: 'cosy' covers only part of it, and the Dutch use it for everything from a café to a family dinner to a well-planned office.
The concept shapes social expectations: hosts arrange lighting, seating and food to create the mood, and guests are expected to contribute to it rather than just consume it.
Gezelligheid is related to German Gemütlichkeit but is more social and less about comfort, and it is often cited as a core part of Dutch identity.
The word appears constantly in everyday speech: a failed party is 'niet gezellig', and an invitation often ends with 'gezellig!'.
exampleEn: A Dutch friend invites you for coffee, lights a candle, puts out one kind of biscuit and says 'gezellig' as you sit down; the compliment is about the atmosphere, not the biscuit.
qualificationEn: The concept is a national self-description as much as an observable fact, and Dutch social life can be both gezellig and highly organised or exclusive; newcomers sometimes find the cosiness hard to enter.

titleEn: How the Netherlands became a country built for bicycles
facts: The Netherlands has around 36,000 km of dedicated cycle paths, and bicycles outnumber people.
Cycling is not just recreation: in Dutch cities a large share of all trips, and a majority of trips to work or school in some areas, are made by bike.
The current system was built after the 1970s, when mass car use and road deaths prompted protests and a policy shift towards protected cycle lanes and traffic calming.
Dutch traffic law gives cyclists priority in many situations, and drivers are usually held liable in collisions with children and cyclists.
Children learn to cycle early and often cycle to school alone, which is one of the most striking differences for visitors.
exampleEn: A four-year-old cycles beside a parent on a separated path to school, locks the bike at the rack, and the parent continues to work by bike.
qualificationEn: The cycling image hides variation: the flat west is not the hilly south, some cities are far better than others, and the Netherlands also has heavy car traffic and conflicts over e-bikes and scooters.

titleEn: Belgium's language border runs through daily life
facts: Belgium has three official languages, Dutch, French and German, but the country is divided into language areas with a fixed border.
The language border was fixed in 1962-63, and constitutional reforms from 1970 onwards turned Belgium into a federal state with separate Flemish, French-speaking and German-speaking communities.
Brussels is officially bilingual, but in practice French dominates, and the surrounding Flemish municipalities have 'facilities' for French speakers that remain politically contested.
Political parties, universities, schools and media are organised separately by language, so the two main communities often consume different news and debate different issues.
The Flemish Movement, which began in the 19th century, fought for Dutch to have equal status with French in education, administration and public life.
exampleEn: A commuter crosses an invisible municipal boundary on the way to Brussels and notices that the road signs and the language of the local government change, even though the streets look identical.
qualificationEn: The border is administrative and political, not a sharp cultural divide: many families are bilingual, Brussels is far more mixed than the map suggests, and the German-speaking community is small but fully institutionalised.

titleEn: The Stammtisch: a table reserved for belonging
facts: A Stammtisch is a regulars' table in a pub or restaurant where the same group meets on a fixed evening, often marked with a sign reserving it.
The word means 'regulars' table', and the institution flourished in the 19th century alongside clubs, choirs and shooting societies.
Traditionally all-male, the Stammtisch was a place for card games such as Skat or Schafkopf, drinking and long political or philosophical arguments.
'Stammtischpolitik' and 'Stammtischniveau' are mildly derogatory terms for simplified, opinionated political talk of the kind heard at such tables.
The ritual is still common in smaller towns and clubs, and it can function as an informal village parliament or support network.
exampleEn: In a Swabian village pub the same eight men occupy the corner table every Thursday, play cards, argue about the local council and reserve the table with a small wooden sign.
qualificationEn: The Stammtisch is declining in big cities and among younger people, and the all-male, beer-and-politics image is a caricature; many groups now include women and meet for other reasons.

titleEn: Co-determination: German workers sit on the board
facts: Germany's co-determination (Mitbestimmung) gives employees rights to representation at work, including seats on the supervisory boards of large companies.
Board-level employee representation exists in a majority of EU and OECD countries in some form, but Germany's system is the most extensive.
In large companies nearly half of supervisory-board seats can be held by employee representatives, alongside a works council that negotiates at plant level.
The system is often credited with Germany's relatively low levels of industrial conflict and with long-term decision-making, though critics say it can slow restructuring.
The Mittelstand, small and medium-sized firms often family-owned, is described as the backbone of the German economy and has its own, less formal traditions of worker involvement.
exampleEn: A machine operator at a German car plant stands for election to the works council; later, an employee representative on the supervisory board questions a factory closure plan.
qualificationEn: Co-determination is not uniform: it applies differently by company size and sector, and the stakeholder model coexists with tough cost-cutting; the Mittelstand is a statistical and cultural category, not a legal one.

sources.title: Worker representation on corporate boards of directors

titleEn: Ostalgie: remembering East Germany one product at a time
facts: Ostalgie is nostalgia for aspects of everyday life in the former German Democratic Republic, from food brands to children's television.
The term is a portmanteau of Ost (east) and Nostalgie and was coined in 1992 by the East German comedian Uwe Steimle.

It became a visible cultural phenomenon in the 1990s and 2000s: Spreewald gherkins, Vita Cola and other eastern products returned to shelves, and films such as Good Bye Lenin! (2003) turned the experience into comedy.
Researchers distinguish nostalgia for things and habits from nostalgia for the political system, and most Ostalgie is about childhood and familiarity rather than a wish to restore the GDR.
The phenomenon also reflects the unequal terms of reunification: East Germans' biographies, qualifications and products were often devalued after 1990.
exampleEn: A Leipzig supermarket sells a brand of mustard that disappeared after 1990 but was relaunched; a grandparent buys it and a grandchild asks what the fuss is about.
qualificationEn: Ostalgie is generation-specific: younger eastern Germans feel it less, western Germans often misread it as political revisionism, and the term is sometimes used to dismiss legitimate complaints about reunification.

titleEn: The döner kebab and the making of Turkish Germany
facts: The döner kebab is meat cooked on a vertical rotisserie, a technique from the 19th-century Ottoman Empire; the modern sandwich version was popularised in 1970s West Berlin by Turkish immigrants.
Germany and Turkey signed a labour recruitment agreement in 1961, bringing 'guest workers' to German industry; many stayed, brought families and built a permanent community.
People of Turkish descent are one of Germany's largest minority groups, with an estimated three million people of full or partial Turkish heritage.
The döner shop became a neighbourhood institution and one of the most visible signs of migration in German cities, alongside the Turkish grocery, bakery and travel agency.
The food is now so thoroughly German that the döner is a standard late-night meal and a subject of price debates and regional rivalries.
exampleEn: In Berlin-Kreuzberg a döner is ordered 'mit alles' and eaten standing up at midnight; the shop is run by a family from Anatolia and the customers are a cross-section of the city.
qualificationEn: 'Turkish Germany' is not one community: it includes Kurds, Alevis, Assyrians and others, and generations differ sharply in language, religion and politics; the döner's origin story is also contested among Berlin vendors.

titleEn: German humour and the stereotype of seriousness
facts: The idea that Germans have no sense of humour is a durable stereotype, and German comedy often plays with it directly.
Germany has a strong tradition of Kabarett, political satire performed in cabarets, which flourished in the Weimar Republic and was suppressed under the Nazis.
Popular humour includes wordplay, regional comedy, carnival speeches and the deadpan sketches of Loriot, whose characters expose the absurdity of German bureaucracy and manners.
The word Schadenfreude entered English from German and is often cited as evidence of a distinctively German comic register.
Regional styles differ: Rhineland carnival, Bavarian folk comedy and Berlin wit are not the same genre, and what Berlin finds funny a Swabian audience may not.
exampleEn: A German colleague replies to a joke with a perfectly straight face, then delivers the punchline; the deadpan delivery is part of the joke, not a sign that it failed.
qualificationEn: The stereotype says more about British and American self-images than about Germany, and German comedy is now diverse: Turkish-German, feminist and internet comedy have changed what audiences laugh at.

titleEn: Why German Sundays stay quiet
facts: Most shops in Germany are closed on Sundays, a rule rooted in the shop-closing law and in the constitutional protection of Sunday and public holidays as days of rest.
Sunday rest is enforced: noisy DIY work, lawn-mowing and some sports are restricted, and neighbours may call the police in serious cases.
The rule has exceptions: bakeries, petrol stations, railway stations and tourist areas can open, and a few 'verkaufsoffene Sonntage' a year are allowed for shopping.
The protected Sunday shapes family life and leisure: visits, walks, church and club activities happen on Sundays, and many Germans defend the closure against commercial pressure.
The debate is ongoing: retail lobbies and some workers want more flexibility, while churches, unions and many citizens defend the day off.
exampleEn: A German family does housework and shopping on Saturday, then spends Sunday walking, visiting relatives and eating cake in the afternoon, with no shops open.
qualificationEn: Sunday closures vary by state and municipality, and online shopping has changed the practical effect; in tourist cities and at stations Sunday can look much like any other day.

titleEn: Du or Sie: the grammar of German distance
facts: German has two pronouns for 'you': du for close, informal relationships and Sie for formal distance, and choosing wrong is a small social event.
The verb forms differ, and the switch from Sie to du usually requires an offer, often from the older or more senior person ('Wir können uns duzen').
Norms vary by context: colleagues in a small team may use du from day one, while a bank or government office keeps Sie, sometimes for decades.
Hybrid forms exist, such as the 'Hamburger Sie' (first name plus Sie), and younger Germans increasingly use du, including at work.
The same tu/vous distinction exists in French and other European languages, but German is unusually explicit about negotiating the switch.
exampleEn: A new employee calls a senior colleague 'Herr Schmidt' for months; after a project dinner the colleague says 'Wir können uns duzen', and the next morning the 'du' feels natural.
qualificationEn: Du/Sie rules differ between Germany, Austria and Switzerland and between regions and generations; many people now use du in more situations, and a wrong pronoun is usually forgiven rather than fatal.

titleEn: The Viennese coffee house rents you a table for hours
facts: The Viennese coffee house (Kaffeehaus) is an institution that shaped Viennese culture, with marble tables, bentwood chairs, newspaper racks and waiters in black.
Since 2011 the 'Viennese coffee house culture' has been listed in Austria's national inventory of intangible cultural heritage.

The culture is defined by the right to sit for hours over a single coffee, reading newspapers or talking; the coffee house is described as a place where time and space are consumed but only the coffee is on the bill.
Each coffee has a name and a specification: a Melange is espresso with milk and foam, an Einspänner is served in a glass with whipped cream, and a 'kleiner Brauner' is coffee with a dash of milk.
In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the coffee house was a workplace for writers, artists and political exiles.
exampleEn: A student orders a Melange, spreads out lecture notes and stays for three hours; the waiter refills the water glass without asking and never brings the bill unrequested.
qualificationEn: The coffee house is partly a nostalgic brand: many traditional houses are now tourist destinations, waiters' formality varies, and younger Viennese drink more to-go coffee than the myth suggests.

titleEn: Röstigraben: the Swiss divide that is not a border
facts: The Röstigraben ('Rösti ditch') is the informal cultural boundary between German-speaking Switzerland and French-speaking Romandy.
The term first appeared during the First World War, when neutral Switzerland sat between the German Empire and the French Republic and the two language communities read different news.
The divide shows up in referendums: French-speaking cantons have often voted differently from German-speaking ones on European integration, immigration and the army.
There is also a Polentagraben between German-speaking Switzerland and the Italian-speaking canton of Ticino, a reminder that the country has four language communities, not two.
The dish itself, Rösti, is a fried potato cake associated with German-speaking Switzerland, and the joke is that the border runs where the menu changes.
exampleEn: On referendum Sunday the map on Swiss television splits between a French-speaking west and a German-speaking east, and commentators immediately discuss the Röstigraben.
qualificationEn: The Röstigraben is a statistical tendency, not a wall: both sides contain internal minorities, cities vote differently from rural areas, and many votes cut across the language divide.

titleEn: Romansh: Switzerland's fourth language in a fight for speakers
facts: Romansh is a Romance language spoken mainly in the Swiss canton of the Grisons (Graubünden), with an estimated 40,000 speakers.
It has been a national language of Switzerland since 1938 and an official language in dealings with Romansh speakers since 1996.
Romansh is itself a bundle of idioms, including Sursilvan, Sutsilvan, Surmiran, Putèr and Vallader, and the standardised Rumantsch Grischun, created in 1982, has been controversial in schools.
The language is used in local schools, radio and television and cantonal administration, but most speakers are bilingual and urbanisation has reduced its everyday base.
Romansh is protected by Swiss minority-language policy and by the canton, which has a language law and funding for cultural projects.
exampleEn: A road sign in Graubünden reads both 'Chur' and 'Cuira', and a grandmother speaks Sursilvan at home while her grandson learns Rumantsch Grischun at school.
qualificationEn: Romansh is threatened rather than dead: speaker numbers are small but stable in some valleys, and the choice between local idioms and a standard language remains a live cultural argument.

titleEn: Schwingen and Hornussen: the Swiss sports under the ski season
facts: Schwingen is a form of folk wrestling native to the pre-alpine, German-speaking parts of Switzerland, also called Hosenlupf ('breeches-lifting').
Wrestlers wear special canvas breeches with belts and win by pinning the opponent's shoulders to the ground.
It is considered a national sport alongside Hornussen, a game in which players hit a puck-like object with a whip, and Steinstossen, stone putting.
The big event is the Eidgenössisches Schwingfest, held every three years, where the winner receives a bull as a prize and is celebrated like a national champion.
Schwingen and Steinstossen are listed in Switzerland's inventory of intangible cultural heritage.
exampleEn: At a cantonal Schwingfest, two farmers in a sawdust-filled circle grip each other's breeches while a brass band plays and the crowd watches from wooden stands.
qualificationEn: Schwingen is regional rather than national in practice: it is strongest in the Bernese Oberland, central and eastern Switzerland, while French- and Italian-speaking regions have other sports and rarely produce champions.

titleEn: Sobremesa: the hour after lunch that Spain keeps
facts: Sobremesa ('upon the table') is the Spanish habit of staying at the table after a meal to talk, drink coffee or a small liqueur, and let the food settle.
It is a social ritual rather than a course: the meal is over, but the table is kept, and nobody is expected to rush off.
The sobremesa hour is a mainstay of Spanish television scheduling, and long Sunday lunches with family can run into the evening.
The habit fits a wider timetable in which lunch is the main meal and dinner is late, often after 21:00.
In cities and workplaces the weekday sobremesa has shrunk, and younger Spaniards often report having less time for it than their grandparents did.
exampleEn: After a Sunday paella a Valencian family stays at the table for two hours over coffee and a bottle of orujo, arguing about football and the grandchildren's exams.
qualificationEn: Sobremesa is more ideal than universal: work schedules, tourism and changing habits have shortened it, and northern Spain's eating rhythms differ from the south.

titleEn: Basque: the European language that has no relatives
facts: Basque (euskara) is a language isolate, unrelated to any other living language, spoken by about 750,000 people in the Basque Country and Navarre.
It survived Roman, Visigothic, Moorish and Castilian domination, and the first surviving written texts are medieval, with earlier place names recorded in Latin and Greek sources.
Under Franco, Basque was banned in public life; since the 1978 constitution it has been co-official in the Basque Country and parts of Navarre.
The standardised language, euskara batua, was created in 1968 to unify dialects, and ikastolas (Basque-language schools) have been central to its revival.
Basque identity and language politics are intertwined, and a higher proportion of young Basques now study in Basque than their parents did.
exampleEn: A child in Bilbao does maths in Basque, speaks Spanish with grandparents and switches to Basque when friends join the table.
qualificationEn: Basque is not spoken uniformly: the Basque Country, Navarre and the French Basque Country have different legal statuses, and Spanish remains dominant in many urban and southern areas.

titleEn: Saudade: why Portuguese longing is not just sadness
facts: Saudade is a Portuguese and Galician word for a melancholic, nostalgic longing for someone or something absent, often with the sense that it may never return.
It derives from the Latin word for solitude, and Portuguese writers have described it as 'memory of something with a desire for it'.
The word is closely associated with fado, the Portuguese song tradition, and with the national self-image of a seafaring people left behind at home.
Brazil officially celebrates a Day of Saudade on 30 January, and the word has entered everyday speech as a way of describing homesickness, love and loss.
It is often called untranslatable, though other languages have words for longing; what is distinctive is the acceptance of pleasure inside the pain.
exampleEn: A Portuguese emigrant in Paris hears a fado in a café and says 'tenho saudade de casa', not simply 'I miss home' but a state of carrying the missing with them.
qualificationEn: The idea that saudade is uniquely Portuguese is a national myth; Galicians use the same word, the emphasis on sentiment varies by generation, and many Portuguese treat the concept with irony.

expression.glossEn: a longing for something absent and loved

titleEn: Italian hand gestures are a second grammar
facts: Hand gestures in Italy function as a parallel system of communication, used alongside speech rather than as a substitute for it.
The gestures form a repertoire with conventional meanings and regional variants, and scholars have catalogued hundreds of them.

The famous pinched-fingers gesture, with the hand raised and the fingers together, is usually glossed as 'What do you want?!' or 'What are you talking about?' and is often exaggerated in foreign portrayals of Italians.
Many gestures have no simple verbal equivalent and carry tone, irony, emphasis, dismissal or admiration, or replace words entirely in noisy settings.
Theories about the origins vary: some trace the repertoire to the many local languages and dialects of the peninsula, others to Mediterranean and Neapolitan performance traditions.
exampleEn: Two friends across a noisy piazza conduct a short conversation entirely with their hands, ending with a shrug and a flick of the wrist that means 'forget it'.
qualificationEn: Not all Italians gesture equally or identically: the repertoire varies by region, generation and context, and the international image of the gesticulating Italian is a caricature that exaggerates a real practice.

expression.glossEn: What do you want?! (said with the pinched-fingers gesture)

titleEn: Xenia: Greek hospitality as a debt to the gods
facts: Xenia is the ancient Greek concept of guest-friendship, an institutionalised relationship of generosity, gift exchange and reciprocity between host and guest.
Hospitality was a moral and religious obligation: Zeus Xenios was the patron of strangers, and refusing a guest could bring divine punishment.
The rituals were formal: the guest was welcomed, fed, bathed and given gifts, and the relationship could be inherited by the next generation.
Homer's Odyssey is built on xenia: the good host Alcinous and the bad hosts, the Cyclops and the suitors, define the moral map of the poem.
Modern Greek uses philoxenia ('love of strangers') for hospitality, and offering food and drink to a visitor remains a strong norm, especially outside big cities.
exampleEn: A stranger arrives at a Greek village house at mealtime and is pressed to sit and eat before anyone asks who they are or why they came.
qualificationEn: The ancient ideal is not a description of modern Greek life: urban Greeks are often too busy to host, the obligation can be felt as pressure by hosts as well as guests, and the 'sacred hospitality' image is partly a national stereotype.

titleEn: In Greece the name day outranks the birthday
facts: A name day celebrates the feast day of the saint a person is named after, and in Greece it is widely celebrated, often more than a birthday.
The custom comes from the Christian calendar of saints: children named after a saint celebrate that saint's day.
Greek children are traditionally named after grandparents, so a name often carries a family history and a saint's protection at once.
On the name day, friends and relatives visit, call or send messages ('Chronia Polla!'), and the person may offer sweets or drinks.
The Orthodox calendar means many name days cluster around major saints' feasts, and common names such as Yannis (St John) or Maria (the Virgin Mary) produce days when half the office is celebrating.
exampleEn: A Greek colleague called Yannis receives calls all morning on 7 January, brings a tray of sweets to the office, and the team wishes him 'Chronia Polla' rather than 'happy birthday'.
qualificationEn: Name days are observed more strongly among older and rural Greeks and among practising Orthodox families; many younger Greeks in cities now treat birthdays as the main celebration.

titleEn: Bread and salt: arriving at a Russian home
facts: In Russia guests are traditionally welcomed with bread and salt, a greeting that signals hospitality and respect; the host offers the bread and the guest takes a piece and dips it in salt.
Visits are planned but generous: hosts lay out a table with tea, jam, pickles and something stronger, and refusing food outright is difficult.
Guests often bring sweets or flowers, in odd numbers for celebrations and even numbers for funerals, and take off their shoes at the door.
The host's generosity is a matter of pride, and the phrase 'chem bogaty, tem i rady' ('we are glad for what we have') frames the table as an offering rather than a performance.
Home visiting became less common in cities during the Soviet period, when people met in kitchens and at dachas, and it is less frequent among younger urban Russians.
exampleEn: A guest arrives with a box of chocolates, takes off their shoes, and is seated at a table already filled with tea, jam and sliced sausage before being asked what they would like.
qualificationEn: The bread-and-salt ceremony is mainly a formal or symbolic welcome today, used for official guests and at weddings; everyday visits differ by family, region and generation and can be much less elaborate.

titleEn: Maltese: Europe's only Semitic official language
facts: Maltese is a Central Semitic language derived from late medieval Sicilian Arabic, and it is the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet.
It is the national language of Malta and the only official Semitic and Afroasiatic language of the European Union.
Maltese has borrowed heavily from Sicilian, Italian and English, and everyday speech mixes Maltese with English ('Maltenglish').
It became an official language in 1934, alongside English, after a long language question in which Italian, English and Maltese competed.
Most Maltese are bilingual in Maltese and English, and English remains the language of many schools, businesses and legal texts.
exampleEn: A Maltese family chats in Maltese at the table, switches to English for a work call and orders in Maltese at the bar, while the sign outside mixes both languages.
qualificationEn: The Semitic label describes the grammar and core vocabulary, not the whole modern lexicon, and Maltese itself has regional dialects; the language is secure at home but under pressure in some professional and media settings.

titleEn: Cyprus: two official languages, two vernaculars, one divided island
facts: The Republic of Cyprus has two official languages, Greek and Turkish; official documents use Standard Modern Greek and Standard Turkish.
In everyday life Greek Cypriots speak Cypriot Greek, a divergent dialect with distinctive vocabulary, phonetics and syntax, while Turkish Cypriots speak Cypriot Turkish.
Since the 1974 division the two communities have largely lived separately, and Greek and Turkish are rarely used across the ceasefire line.
The constitution recognises Armenian and Cypriot Arabic (Maronite) as minority languages, and Armenian Cypriots and Maronites maintain their own schools and churches.
English is widely used in business, higher education and tourism and is the common language of many mixed or international settings.
exampleEn: A Nicosia shopkeeper speaks Cypriot Greek to a customer, switches to English for a tourist and reads a Greek-language newspaper at the counter.
qualificationEn: Language in Cyprus is inseparable from politics: describing Cypriot Greek and Cypriot Turkish as dialects is standard, but the division means the two vernaculars have developed separately for decades.

titleEn: Andorra: a country that runs on Catalan
facts: Andorra is the only state in the world where Catalan is the sole official language.
Andorra is essentially Catalan-speaking, and Catalan is the language of parliament, schools, administration and most media.
The constitution of 1993 made Catalan official and established Andorra as a parliamentary co-principality.
The school system is plural: Andorran, Spanish and French curricula coexist, so children may be taught in Catalan, Spanish or French depending on the school.
A large share of residents are foreign nationals, and many speak Spanish or Portuguese at home while using Catalan in public life.
exampleEn: A child in an Andorran school writes in Catalan, goes home to a Spanish-speaking family and switches to French for a ski lesson with a visiting instructor.
qualificationEn: Andorra's language is secure in law, but its small population and dependence on immigration mean Spanish is widely heard, and the three school systems produce different levels of Catalan.

titleEn: San Marino's six-month captains and the oldest republic
facts: San Marino is a microstate surrounded by Italy, claiming to have been founded in 301 AD by the stonecutter Marinus and often called the world's oldest surviving republic.
Its two heads of state are the Captains Regent, elected every six months by the Great and General Council.
The investiture ceremony takes place on 1 April and 1 October each year, and the tradition dates back at least to 1243.
The diarchy is derived from the Roman consuls: two equal heads of state who hold no executive power and serve short terms to prevent the accumulation of power.
The Captains Regent are chosen from coalition parties, and the office is a civic ritual as much as a government post, with processions in historical costume.
exampleEn: On 1 April the square in front of the Palazzo Pubblico fills with crossbowmen and officials as the new Captains Regent take office for six months.
qualificationEn: The 'oldest republic' claim is a national tradition rather than a settled historical fact, and the Captains Regent's powers are largely ceremonial; San Marino's politics are dominated by the Great and General Council and by Italy's influence.

titleEn: Wigilia: Poland's Christmas Eve is the main event
facts: Wigilia is the Polish Christmas Eve supper on 24 December, and for many families it is more important than Christmas Day itself.
The meal traditionally begins when the first star appears and is meatless: typical dishes include carp, herring, pierogi, beetroot soup and dried-fruit compote.
An opłatek (Christmas wafer) is shared at the table, with each person breaking off a piece and exchanging wishes.
An empty place is often set for an unexpected guest or for absent relatives, a custom linked to hospitality and memory.
Pasterka, the midnight Mass, follows the supper in Catholic churches, and 'Wesołych Świąt' wishes are exchanged.
exampleEn: A Polish family sets twelve dishes on the table, shares the opłatek, leaves one chair empty and then goes to Pasterka at midnight.
qualificationEn: The twelve-dish rule is a folk ideal rather than a universal practice, and regional and family customs vary widely; in cities and among younger Poles the supper may be shorter and the religious element weaker.

titleEn: Czechia: the European country that stopped going to church
facts: In the 2021 census 47.8% of Czechs declared themselves irreligious, while 21.3% described themselves as believers and only 11.7% identified with Christianity.
In the first half of the 20th century more than 90% of Czechs were Christians, so the change is one of the fastest religious collapses in Europe.
The communist period from 1948 to 1989 promoted atheism and restricted the churches, but the decline began earlier and continued after 1989.
Czech secularism is visible in everyday life: empty churches, civil weddings and funerals, and a public culture in which religion is largely a private matter.
Christmas and Easter remain important cultural holidays, but for many Czechs they are family and food occasions rather than religious ones.
exampleEn: A Czech family celebrates Christmas with carp and presents, argues about the television schedule, and nobody attends a church service.
qualificationEn: Czechia is not uniformly atheist: religious practice is higher in Moravia, in some rural areas and among believers who keep their faith private, and surveys also show interest in alternative spirituality.

titleEn: The fujara: a shepherd's instrument that became a national symbol
facts: The fujara is a large overtone fipple flute from central Slovakia, typically 160-200 cm long and tuned in A, G or F.
It has three tone holes on the lower part of the body and a parallel air channel (vzduchovod) that feeds the fipple, giving a deep, contrabass sound.
It originated as a shepherd's instrument, played alone in the mountains and used for long, meditative melodies with rhythmic breathing.
Fujara music is performed at folk festivals and has been recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
The instrument's revival is associated with the folk-music movement and with makers who carve and decorate the flutes in the villages around Podpoľanie.
exampleEn: A shepherd at a summer festival plays a fujara solo while the audience falls silent; the melody is built on long notes and overtones rather than chords.
qualificationEn: The fujara is a regional instrument, not a national one: it belongs to central Slovakia, many Slovaks have never seen one played live, and the UNESCO listing protects a tradition that was nearly lost.

titleEn: Hungarian names put the family before the person
facts: Hungarian uses Eastern name order: the family name comes first in both speech and writing, so the physicist is 'Farkas Bertalan', not 'Bertalan Farkas'.
Hungarian is one of the few national languages in Europe to use this order, alongside some Basque nationalist usage and, outside Europe, Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese.
The order is reversed when Hungarians are written about in languages that use Western order, which can confuse visitors.
Hungarian dates are also written year-month-day, and formal documents follow the same pattern.
Married women have traditionally used a -né suffix attached to the husband's name, and a 2022 law allows a wider choice of married names.
exampleEn: A Hungarian passport lists 'Nagy Anna', and an English-language conference badge prints 'Anna Nagy'; the family name is the same, but the convention is reversed.
qualificationEn: Hungarian name order is consistent in Hungarian, but many Hungarians adapt their names for foreign audiences, and some names, especially of foreign origin, do not follow the pattern neatly.

titleEn: Mărțișor: March begins with a red-and-white thread
facts: Mărțișor is a spring tradition in Romania and Moldova: a small object tied with intertwined red and white strings, given on 1 March.
The word is the diminutive of marț, an old folk name for March, and literally means 'little March'.
The custom is linked to Roman New Year celebrations on 1 March and to the arrival of spring; the red thread stands for vitality and the white for purity or snow.
In the modern practice, women and girls receive the mărțișor and wear it pinned to clothing during the first part of March.
The tradition was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2017, jointly with the similar Bulgarian martenitsa and related practices in North Macedonia and Moldova.
exampleEn: On 1 March a Romanian grandfather gives his granddaughter a small silver horseshoe tied with red and white thread, and she pins it to her coat.
qualificationEn: Mărțișor is shared across borders and closely related to Bulgarian, Macedonian and Greek spring customs; its form and meaning vary by region and family, and the UNESCO listing covers a set of related practices rather than a single uncontested tradition.

titleEn: Baba Marta and the martenitsa ritual of March
facts: Baba Marta ('Granny March') is a Bulgarian mythical figure who brings the end of winter and the beginning of spring, celebrated on 1 March.
On that day Bulgarians exchange and wear martenitsi: small red-and-white yarn ornaments, often in the shape of two dolls, Pizho (white) and Penda (red).
The martenitsa is worn until the wearer sees a stork, a swallow or a blossoming tree, then tied to a fruit tree or placed under a stone for a fortune-telling game.
The custom is very old and pre-Christian in origin, with regional variants across Bulgaria.
In 2017 UNESCO inscribed the related cultural practices of 1 March in Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Moldova and Romania.
exampleEn: On 1 March a Bulgarian child is given a woven red-and-white doll by a grandparent and wears it on the wrist until the first stork is spotted.
qualificationEn: Baba Marta is a folk figure, not a religious saint, and observance varies between families; in cities the martenitsa is often exchanged as a small gift rather than lived as a calendar ritual.

titleEn: The vyshyvanka as an everyday national statement
facts: A vyshyvanka is an embroidered shirt in Ukrainian and Belarusian national costume, and in Ukraine the embroidery patterns are specific to regions and families.

The shirt moved from village dress to national symbol: embroidered shirts were worn by writers and dissidents in the Soviet era and became a mass symbol during the 2004 Orange Revolution and after 2014.
Vyshyvanka Day, started in 2006, is marked on the third Thursday of May, when people wear embroidered shirts to work and school.
The patterns are not merely decorative: motifs of oak, grapes, roosters and geometric forms carry symbolic meanings, and colour choices vary by region.
After the 2022 Russian invasion, the vyshyvanka became a conspicuous sign of identity at home and in the diaspora.
exampleEn: On Vyshyvanka Day a Kyiv office fills with colleagues in embroidered shirts, and a grandfather lends his grandson a shirt embroidered by his own mother.
qualificationEn: The vyshyvanka is a living garment with many regional styles, but its current symbolic use is modern and politicised; not all Ukrainians own or wear one, and the Soviet period both suppressed and commercialised the tradition.

titleEn: The dacha: Russia's weekend second life
facts: A dacha is a seasonal or year-round second home in the exurbs of post-Soviet countries, especially Russia.
The word comes from the verb davat ('to give') and originally referred to land allotted by the tsar to his nobles.
In the Soviet period, dachas and allotment plots were distributed to citizens by local authorities and enterprises, and the small plot with a simple house became a mass phenomenon.
Dachniki spend weekends and summers growing vegetables, berries and flowers, and the dacha is as much a social world as a property.
The typical Soviet dacha plot was six sotki (600 square metres), and many settlements still have a collective water supply and a strong sense of neighbourliness.
exampleEn: On Friday evening a Moscow family takes the suburban train to a wooden house with a vegetable patch, where the grandmother has been living since May.
qualificationEn: The dacha is not one thing: some are luxury houses, some are tiny wooden huts, and younger Russians increasingly use them for leisure rather than food production; the six-sotki image is the Soviet norm, not the current reality.

titleEn: The Russian anekdot and the habit of political irony
facts: Russian jokes (anekdoty) are short fictional stories or dialogues with a punchline, built around fixed settings and recurring characters.
Categories include Vovochka the schoolboy, the Chukchi (a northern people used as a naive outsider), the Armenian Radio and generic characters such as the husband, wife and mother-in-law.
Political jokes were a major genre in the Soviet era, often told in kitchens and on the phone, and they functioned as covert commentary on shortages, censorship and leaders.
Many jokes rely on linguistic puns and wordplay that are untranslatable, and some have travelled into other languages in adapted form.
The genre continues on the internet, but the old Soviet characters are fading from use among younger Russians.
exampleEn: An Armenian Radio joke asks a question and gives a punchline that comments on a shortage; listeners laugh at the bureaucratic absurdity rather than at a person.
qualificationEn: The genre is not a reliable guide to what Russians think: jokes circulate in private, political humour has become riskier under current conditions, and the 'Russian melancholy' image is as much a Western stereotype as a local self-description.

titleEn: Klapa: Dalmatian singing with no instruments at all
facts: Klapa is a form of traditional a cappella singing from Dalmatia, and the word translates as 'a group of friends'.
It grew partly from church singing, and the songs are usually about love, wine, the sea and the homeland.
The music is built on harmony and melody; rhythm is secondary, and a typical group has several male or female voices with a lead singer.
In 2012 klapa singing was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Festivals, especially in Omiš, have kept the tradition alive, and there are both traditional groups and modern staged performances.
exampleEn: At a summer festival in a Dalmatian town, a men's klapa sings in close harmony on a stone square, and the audience knows the choruses well enough to hum along.
qualificationEn: Klapa is closely tied to the Dalmatian coast and islands, not to Croatia as a whole, and the festival repertoire has been standardised by competition; inland Croatians may barely know it.

titleEn: Slava: a family's saint day, inherited through the generations
facts: Slava is a Serbian Orthodox tradition in which a family gathers on the feast day of its patron saint.
The saint is inherited patrilineally, so a family's slava usually passes from father to son, and the date is fixed by the church calendar.
The ritual includes a special bread (slavski kolač), a candle, boiled wheat (koljivo), red wine and incense, and it can range from strict church observance to a relaxed family party.
Guests are welcomed and fed, and the slava is an occasion for reaffirming family and neighbourhood ties.
In 2014 the Slava was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
exampleEn: On his family's slava a Serbian man lights the candle, cuts the bread with the priest or eldest family member, and then serves rakija and food to relatives and neighbours.
qualificationEn: Slava is primarily a Serbian Orthodox practice with variations among families and regions; it is not universal among all Serbs, and urban families may celebrate more modestly than the village ideal.

titleEn: The kafana and the long Serbian evening
facts: A kafana is a coffeehouse, bistro or tavern common in Southeast Europe, originally serving coffee and warm drinks and now usually alcohol and food as well.
The concept spread during Ottoman rule and evolved into a social gathering place, traditionally for men, where coffee, rakija and conversation went together.
Many kafanas feature live music, and the kafana is associated with Serbian folk and brass music, long nights and emotional singing.
The word comes from the Turkish kahvehane (coffee house), and similar institutions exist across the Balkans under different names.
Kafanas have been political and literary meeting places, and they remain a symbol of a particular kind of slow, sociable evening.
exampleEn: A group of friends meets at a Belgrade kafana at nine, orders grilled food and rakija, and stays until the band packs up after two in the morning.
qualificationEn: The kafana is a regional Balkan institution rather than a Serbian invention, and the smoky-tavern image is partly nostalgic; smoking bans, prices and younger drinking habits have changed the scene.

titleEn: Sevdalinka: Bosnia's slow song of love and loss
facts: Sevdalinka, also called sevdah, is a traditional genre of urban folk song from Bosnia and Herzegovina, closely associated with Bosniak culture and spread across the former Yugoslavia.
The songs are slow and melismatic, usually about love, longing and separation, and the word sevdah derives from the Arabic and Turkish word for love or passion.
Many sevdalinkas are anonymous and were passed down orally, while the composers of the best-known versions are often known.
The genre developed in Ottoman-era Bosnian towns, with instruments such as the saz and later the accordion, and is now performed by singers with small ensembles.
In 2024 sevdalinka was added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
exampleEn: At a Sarajevo café a singer performs 'Kad ja pođoh na Bembašu' with accordion and guitar, and the older guests sing the refrain quietly from their tables.
qualificationEn: Sevdalinka is shared across Bosnia, Serbia, Croatia and Montenegro and is associated with Bosniak identity in particular; the genre's 'Oriental' image is partly a later construction, and pop arrangements have changed how it sounds.

titleEn: Besa: the Albanian word that binds a promise
facts: Besa (indefinite form besë) is an Albanian cultural precept usually translated as 'pledge of honour', 'solemn faith' or 'word of honour', and regarded as sacred and inviolable.
It is a cornerstone of Albanian traditional customary law, the Kanun, which regulated tribal society orally for centuries.
The adjective besnik, derived from besa, means 'faithful' or 'trustworthy', and Besa and Besnik remain popular Albanian given names.
Besa carried practical obligations: a person who gave besa was expected to protect a guest, keep a promise or guarantee a truce, even at personal cost.
The concept is often cited in accounts of Albanians sheltering Jews during the Second World War, and 'Besa' has been used as a moral reference in modern Albanian public life.
exampleEn: Two families in a blood feud agree to a besa for a wedding; for the duration of the celebration no one may touch a weapon or seek revenge.
qualificationEn: The romantic image of besa can obscure the harshness of the customary code it belongs to, including blood feud and patriarchal rules; modern Albanians use the word in everyday speech for a promise, not only in the heroic sense.

expression.glossEn: a pledge of honour; a promise that must be kept

titleEn: Macedonian: standardised in 1945, contested ever since
facts: Macedonian is an Eastern South Slavic language spoken as a first language by around 1.7 million people and the official language of North Macedonia.
It was standardised in 1944-45 on the basis of central dialects, after the creation of the Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia.

Most linguists outside Bulgaria treat Macedonian as a separate South Slavic standard, while Bulgarian linguists have often described it as a dialect of Bulgarian, and the dispute has been politically charged.

The country's name dispute with Greece from 1991 to 2019 was resolved by the Prespa Agreement of 2018, under which the state became North Macedonia; language recognition disputes with Bulgaria continued afterwards.
Macedonian is recognised as a minority language in parts of Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo, and it has a literary tradition, media and universities.
exampleEn: A student in Skopje reads a Macedonian novel for class, watches a Macedonian-language news broadcast and hears Bulgarian objections to the language's status on social media.
qualificationEn: The language itself is not in doubt, since people speak it, but its political classification is contested; the number of speakers and the reach of Macedonian in the diaspora are also difficult to measure.

titleEn: Slovenia's beekeeping culture and the birthday of World Bee Day
facts: Slovenia has a strong beekeeping tradition, and the native Carniolan honey bee (Apis mellifera carnica) is prized for its gentleness and is used by beekeepers around the world.
Anton Janša, an 18th-century Slovene beekeeper and imperial teacher in Vienna, is regarded as a pioneer of modern apiculture; he was born on 20 May.
In 2017 the UN General Assembly proclaimed 20 May World Bee Day on a proposal from Slovenia, and the first observance was in 2018.
Beekeeping is a national pastime: Slovenia has a high density of beekeepers, and hives are kept in gardens and on rooftops as well as in apiaries.
Painted beehive panels (panjske končnice), a folk art form from the 18th and 19th centuries, are part of the country's cultural heritage and are now reproduced as souvenirs.
exampleEn: In a Slovenian village a family tends a row of painted hives at the end of the garden, and in May the local beekeeping society holds an open day.
qualificationEn: Slovenia's beekeeping is modern and commercial as well as traditional, and the World Bee Day campaign is a diplomatic success story that does not mean all is well for pollinators; honeybee health and wild pollinators are different issues.

titleEn: Roma: Europe's largest minority and the language that holds it together
facts: The Roma are Europe's largest ethnic minority, estimated at 10-12 million people across the continent.
Linguistic and genetic evidence suggests origins in north-western India, with westward migration reaching Europe around the 13th and 14th centuries.
Romani is an Indo-Aryan macrolanguage with major dialect groups such as Balkan Romani, Vlax Romani and Sinte Romani; many communities also speak mixed Para-Romani varieties.
The 1971 World Romani Congress adopted a common flag and anthem, and 'Roma' became the preferred collective name in international institutions.

Roma communities were enslaved in the Romanian principalities until the mid-19th century and persecuted under the Nazis in the Porajmos; today they face widespread segregation in housing, education and employment.
exampleEn: In a Slovak village, children from a Roma settlement attend a segregated school while their parents look for work abroad and send money home.
qualificationEn: Roma are not a single community: language, religion, occupation and legal status vary enormously between and within countries, and many people described as Roma by outsiders do not use that label themselves.

titleEn: Joik: singing a person, not about one
facts: A joik is a traditional Sámi song form in which the performer evokes a person, animal or place rather than singing about it.
The word covers several regional singing styles, and a performer is called a joikaaja, joiker or jojkare depending on the language.
Joik has no necessary lyrics: it is built from short motifs, repetition and distinctive vocal timbre, and it can be performed alone or in a group.
Christian missionaries treated joik as pagan and discouraged it, and the tradition survived partly through families and local communities; it is now performed at festivals and in contemporary music.
Sámi musicians have brought joik into pop, rock and film music, and the style is one marker of Sámi identity across Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
exampleEn: At a Sámi festival a performer joiks a relative's name, and listeners recognise the person from the melody before anyone explains who it is.
qualificationEn: Joik is not a single genre: regional styles, personal ownership of joiks and the boundary between traditional and modern performance are all debated within Sámi communities, and outsiders often mistake it for a form of singing about nature.

titleEn: British Asians and the making of Brick Lane
facts: In the 2021 census 5.76 million people, or 8.6% of the UK population, identified as Asian or Asian British.
Post-war labour shortages brought migrants from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and the 1972 expulsion of Asians from Uganda added a further wave of families.
Brick Lane in east London became the centre of a Bangladeshi community, with curry houses, a mosque and a street market; its earlier Huguenot and Jewish history is still visible in the buildings.

The label 'British Asian' was popularised in the 1980s and covers very different communities, languages and religions, including Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Sri Lankan and East African Asian families.
Brick Lane has been a battleground over gentrification, licensing and cultural ownership, and the curry-house trade has declined as younger generations move into other work.
exampleEn: On a Sunday morning a Bangladeshi family shops for vegetables on Brick Lane while tourists photograph the street art and a restaurant tout offers a curry deal.
qualificationEn: 'British Asian' is a broad political and census category, not a community: Bangladeshis, Indians, Pakistanis and others differ in language, class and religion, and the Brick Lane story is specific to one London neighbourhood.

titleEn: Vietnamese Czechs and the corner shop
facts: Vietnamese people are the third-largest ethnic minority in the Czech Republic after Slovaks and Ukrainians, and the largest Asian group, with more than 38,000 people in the 2021 census.
Large-scale Vietnamese settlement began in the 1950s and 1960s, when Czechoslovakia invited students and workers from North Vietnam, and continued through the 1980s.
After 1989 many Vietnamese stayed and opened small shops, especially the potraviny corner grocery, which became a fixture of Czech towns and villages.
The community is often described through the '1.5 generation', young people who arrived as children and move between Vietnamese and Czech worlds.
Vietnamese-language schools, Buddhist pagodas and business networks maintain community life, while the second generation increasingly enters Czech universities and professions.
exampleEn: A Czech customer buys vegetables and beer at a Vietnamese potraviny at 9 p.m., and the owner's daughter, born in Prague, translates between her parents and the supplier.
qualificationEn: The corner-shop stereotype flattens a diverse community that includes students, professionals and second-generation Czechs; the Vietnamese population is also relatively small and concentrated in towns where shops were available.

titleEn: Albanians in Switzerland: the diaspora next door
facts: Albanians in Switzerland mostly trace their origins to Kosovo, North Macedonia and, to a lesser extent, Albania and other Albanian-speaking territories.
While moderate numbers of Yugoslav citizens lived in Switzerland in the 1980s, the bulk of Albanian immigration came in the 1990s and 2000s, especially during and after the Kosovo war.
The community is one of the largest immigrant groups in Switzerland, and Albanian is among the most widely spoken non-national languages in the country.
Second-generation Albanians are prominent in Swiss football and public life, and players such as Granit Xhaka and Xherdan Shaqiri have become symbols of dual identity.
Remittances and family ties connect the diaspora to Kosovo and North Macedonia, and integration debates in Switzerland often focus on language, education and Islam.
exampleEn: A Swiss-Albanian teenager speaks Swiss German at school, Albanian at home and watches a Kosovo match with cousins on the weekend.
qualificationEn: The community is not homogeneous: Kosovar, Macedonian and Albanian origins carry different histories, and citizenship, language and religion vary; the football-celebrity image highlights only one successful strand of a much broader migration.

titleEn: The emptying European village
facts: Rural flight is the movement of people from the countryside to cities, driven by mechanised agriculture, fewer services and the search for work and education.

In southern and eastern Europe the pattern is visible in abandoned houses and ageing populations: Spain's 'emptied Spain', Italy's one-euro house schemes and Portugal's interior are the best-known examples.
Europe as a whole is ageing: lower fertility and longer life expectancy are shrinking the working-age population and expanding the number of retired people.
Small villages lose schools, shops, buses and doctors first, which makes it harder for those who remain, often older women, to stay.
Governments and the EU respond with rural development funds, broadband projects and relocation incentives, but the demographic trend has not reversed.
exampleEn: In a village in inland Spain, the school closes when the last child leaves, the bus service is cut to twice a week, and the remaining residents are mostly over 70.
qualificationEn: Rural flight is not uniform: some rural areas near cities are growing through commuting and tourism, while others empty; the 'abandoned village' image can hide active communities and local resistance.

titleEn: Two clocks: punctuality in Europe is a rule, not a fact
facts: Deadlines and meeting times have different social meanings across Europe: in much of the north, arriving a few minutes late requires an apology, while in parts of the south the same arrival may be unremarkable.
The academic quarter shows the convention can be institutional: in Swedish and Finnish universities, lectures traditionally begin 15 minutes after the stated hour.

Switzerland and Germany are associated with extreme punctuality, but Swiss public transport runs to a published timetable while German trains often do not, so norms and infrastructure are different things.
Stereotypes are unreliable: rural Germans may be less punctual than Hamburg bankers, and a Rome business meeting can start on time while a Roman dinner invitation does not.
The north-south contrast is a shorthand people use to explain each other, not a rule that individuals follow consistently.
exampleEn: A Finnish student arrives at 10:15 for a 10:00 lecture and is not late; the same student arrives at 10:00 for a German meeting and is late enough to apologise.
qualificationEn: Countries are not clocks: class, age, city size and context (work versus private invitation) change the rules more than nationality does, and many northerners are relaxed about time while many southerners are strict.
